processing: Single buds withered and dried, without firing or rolling, as in Fujian silver needle but from Yunnan large-leaf plants.
harvest_season: Spring, as for silver needle generally; the buds are picked before they open.
appearance_dry: Long, fat buds with grey-silver down, larger than most Fujian needles.
appearance_wet: Thick, plump whole buds, pale green-yellow.
taste_profile: Little is written on it as a named tea. Yunnan white tea is generally sweet and mellow, and large-leaf buds usually carry more weight than a Fuding needle.

brewing.notes: Same logic as any silver needle: buds extract slowly, so give them time. These thick buds can take slightly hotter water than Fujian needles.

vintage_note: Usually sold as a spring harvest of a named year. Some lots are kept and aged as with other Yunnan white tea. The silver needle name is used loosely here, and Fujian's traditional name is not the same thing, so check the origin on the label.
description:
Yunnan Silver Needle is the Yunnan answer to Fujian's famous all-bud white tea: single buds, withered and dried, but from large-leaf plants far from Fuding. In a shop list it may sit alongside Yue Guang Bai buds, and the name is not a strict one.

The method is the classic one, and the plant makes the difference. Large-leaf buds are generally fatter than Fujian needles and tend to give more body.

Treat it gently at first, and let the steeps grow longer as the buds open.

Be careful about any claim that a Yunnan bud tea is the same as Fujian Bai Hao Yin Zhen; compare it instead as its own thing.
history: Little is documented about Yunnan Silver Needle as a named tea. It appears mostly as a trade name among exporters. When sellers began using the silver needle name for Yunnan buds is not recorded.
